sections.heading: What is postpartum depression?
paragraphs: Postpartum (or postnatal) depression is a depressive illness that can develop during pregnancy or at any point in the first year after giving birth. It affects many mothers and can also affect fathers and partners.

It is different from the “baby blues”, the short period of tearfulness and mood swings that many mothers feel in the first two weeks after birth. When low mood lasts longer than two weeks, or starts to affect daily life, it may be depression and deserves attention.

sections.heading: Common signs and symptoms
paragraphs: Every mother's experience is different, but these signs are common and can signal that it's time to seek support:
bullets: Persistent sadness, emptiness or hopelessness for more than two weeks
Losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy
Feeling anxious, panicky or constantly worried, including intrusive thoughts about the baby
Difficulty bonding with your baby or feeling detached
Sleep or appetite changes beyond what a newborn explains
Strong feelings of guilt, shame or being a “bad mother”
Exhaustion that makes everyday tasks feel impossible
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby: please seek help immediately

sections.heading: When it's an emergency
paragraphs: Postpartum psychosis is rare but serious. Signs include confusion, hallucinations, paranoia, extreme mood swings or thoughts that seem out of character, usually in the first weeks after birth. It is a medical emergency: call your local emergency number or go to an emergency department straight away. The same applies to any thoughts of ending your life or harming your baby.

sections.heading: What increases the risk?
paragraphs: Postpartum depression can affect anyone. Some factors make it more likely:
bullets: A personal or family history of depression, anxiety or bipolar disorder
Stressful life events, financial pressure or relationship difficulties
Limited practical or emotional support
A difficult pregnancy or birth, premature birth or a baby needing intensive care
Sleep deprivation and the physical demands of recovery

sections.heading: Why early detection matters
paragraphs: Recognising symptoms early means support can start sooner, which improves recovery and reduces the impact on the whole family. Validated screening tools such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) are widely used by health services around the world to help identify mothers who may need further assessment.
bullets: Notice changes in your mood, sleep and energy over time
Ask your partner or family whether they've noticed changes
Complete a screening questionnaire and share the result with your midwife or GP
Keep your routine postnatal check-ups

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
paragraphs: Postpartum depression is treatable. Depending on how you feel, your care team may suggest talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, support groups, medication that is compatible with breastfeeding, or a combination. Most mothers recover fully with the right support.

sections.heading: Everyday coping strategies
bullets: Rest whenever you can and accept offers of practical help
Eat regularly and drink enough water
Get outside for short walks and daylight
Stay connected with people you trust, even briefly
Write down your feelings to make sense of them
Let go of perfection. “Good enough” is truly enough
